For most of the last two decades, trucking could read the politics of its workforce fights along a familiar line, with one party broadly friendly to the independent contractor model and the other broadly skeptical of it, but according to the policy and legal experts who briefed an American Trucking Associations committee at the group’s recent conference, that map is being redrawn in a way that should make every fleet operator uneasy regardless of their own politics, because the pressure on how trucking classifies and uses its workforce is now coming from both sides of the aisle at once.
The headline numbers alone guarantee change. There are 36 gubernatorial elections in 2026, and 17 of those are effectively open seats where a governor is term-limited or retiring, which historically produces more movement. On the legislative side, 88 of the country’s 99 state legislative chambers are up for election. Layer in a round of midterm redistricting and a genuinely contested set of races, and the experts cautioned that the partisan landscape could shift more after this cycle than it has in several. For an industry whose labor rules are increasingly written at the state and local level, that is a lot of ground moving at once.
The States To Watch
The legal team from Scopelitis , which tracks this terrain closely for the industry, flagged a specific set of states where the outcomes carry the most potential to change the rules trucking operates under. On the legislative side, the ones to watch are Alaska, Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. On the gubernatorial side, the races that have settled into genuine toss-up status are Georgia, Nevada, Wisconsin, and Ohio, with Alaska, Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, Oregon, Florida, Kansas, and Texas also worth monitoring.
There is a reason the same handful of industrial and Upper Midwest states keep appearing. These are the places where the workforce-classification question is most actively contested, where a change in a governor’s office or a flip in a legislative chamber can move quickly from an election result to a new rule about who can be an independent contractor and who must be an employee.
The Realignment That Changes Everything
The deeper story, and the one the experts spent the most time on, is not which party controls what. It is a realignment inside both parties that is converging on the same place.
On the Republican side, a growing bloc of what the ATA’s Capitol Hill team described as pro-worker populist conservatives has emerged. The team was careful to draw a distinction that matters here. These members are pro-worker, not pro-labor. They are not endorsing the agenda of the labor unions. Rather, they are trying to win the votes of working-class Americans who feel the unions have abandoned them, and their instinct is skepticism of large corporations. The practical effect, though, is that this group has been unwilling to back legislation the trucking industry considers straightforward and business-friendly, and the team said the bloc now stretches well beyond the Rust Belt states where it started, with members from across the country.
That shift has already stalled the industry’s federal priorities. The Modern Worker Empowerment Act, which would amend federal labor law to replace the shifting multi-factor classification test with a single, stable common-law standard, is the industry’s attempt to end the whipsaw in which every change of administration flips the rules. It was introduced by Representative Kevin Kiley of California, a longtime ally on this issue, and it cleared its House committee only after the industry was asked to personally lobby multiple Republican members to secure a party-line vote. It then stalled in the Senate. A separate bill narrowing the joint-employer standard, the Save Local Business Act introduced by Representative James Comer, was pulled from the House floor when Republican leadership realized that roughly 20 of its own members would not support it.
On the Democratic side, the briefing described rising momentum from progressive and self-described democratic socialist members who are capitalizing on the same working-class frustration, including leadership challenges aimed at long-tenured members. The result is that pro-worker Republicans and pro-labor Democrats increasingly share mutual interest on certain labor policies, even as they compete for the same voters. The ATA team’s blunt prediction was that this convergence means there will be no federal legislative movement to lock in an industry-friendly classification standard, which leaves the uncertainty the industry most wants to end firmly in place.
It Is Fair To Note The Other Side
This is a contested policy debate, and it is worth stating the case that the industry’s critics make, because it explains why the realignment has teeth.
Worker advocates and many state lawmakers argue that the independent contractor model, as used across parts of the gig and logistics economy, can leave workers without the protections employees receive, from unemployment insurance to workers’ compensation, and that tightening classification or extending some benefits to contractors corrects a real imbalance. That view is driving developments like portable benefits, a concept gaining traction at the state level that would attach retirement, healthcare, or reserve-account benefits to the worker rather than the employer. The industry is not uniformly opposed to the idea, and the Scopelitis team noted that the design details decide everything, with voluntary, flexible models drawing far less industry objection than rigid, mandatory state-fund versions that failed in Hawaii and Washington. The point is not that one side is right, but that the political energy behind reclassification is now bipartisan enough that trucking cannot count on either party to simply hold the line.
The Regulatory Counterweight, And Why It Is Not Enough
There is some movement in the industry’s favor, but it illustrates exactly why elections matter so much. The Department of Labor is moving toward a clearer independent contractor rule built on two core factors, the level of control the hiring entity exercises and whether the worker has a genuine entrepreneurial opportunity for profit and loss. The industry expects that rule to be published late in 2026 with a 60-day implementation window, and it includes language favorable to trucking, such as clarifying that contract terms requiring compliance with the law and with health and safety rules do not count as the kind of control that destroys contractor status. The ATA has also petitioned the National Labor Relations Board to adopt a similar standard.
But a regulation is only as durable as the administration that writes it. This same rule has ping-ponged between administrations for years, which is precisely why the industry has been chasing a permanent legislative fix, and precisely why the stalling of that legislation matters. What an election can give, the next election can take back.
Where The Real Action Moves
The experts closed with a warning that the most consequential changes may not happen in Washington or even in state capitals at all. As state legislatures grow more lopsided and gridlocked, the action is shifting to administrative agencies and city and local councils, which can move fast and with less visibility. T hey pointed to delivery-protection measures advancing in New York City and Chicago, some of which would require last-mile deliveries to be performed by employees rather than contractors, and to New Jersey’s recently effective regulation consolidating the ABC test across a wide range of employment statutes. The caution for operators was direct. By the time you hear about a local rule, it is often already done, and it can reshape your labor model overnight.
Why It Matters
The usual assumption that trucking’s workforce rules swing cleanly with one party or the other no longer holds, because a pro-worker Republican bloc and a pro-labor Democratic bloc are converging on more scrutiny of the independent contractor model at the same time, which means the pressure on how fleets classify and deploy labor is likely to grow no matter who wins in 2026. For fleet and finance leaders, the takeaway is that uncertainty itself is now the planning constant, so the smart posture is to watch the specific state, agency, and local arenas where these rules are actually being written, and to build a workforce model that can withstand scrutiny under a tightening standard rather than betting on a friendly election to hold the status quo in place.
This article is based on presentations by Scopelitis attorneys and American Trucking Associations government affairs and regulatory staff at an ATA policy committee session, and reflects the political analysis and predictions presented there. Characterizations of pending legislation and political dynamics are as described by the presenters.
